parents.course: Introduction to the Study of Literature and Culture

ns2:section.sectionText: SP25 - ENGL 200 - Intro to Literature and Culture - Lori Newcomb - In this course, we sample the breadth of imaginative writing in English with a specific purpose: to develop precise tools of literary analysis that are adaptable across forms, genres, and periods. We also take time to ponder some fundamental questions. What decides whether a text counts as “literature”? What can literature do for its readers? How does literature try to move cultures forward? Why does literature get banned? How can literary analysis advance social justice, whether applied to past or current texts? Literature can happen anytime and anywhere, and our readings are inclusive in terms of gender, nationality, race and ethnicity, genre and medium, and historical period. Among other adventures, we’ll read lyric poetry from the English Renaissance, the Harlem Renaissance, and the Chicago Renaissance; classic short stories and two very moving recent American novels; and a genuinely surprising play by Shakespeare that we’ll also see performed at UI's Krannert Center. Alongside our reading and viewing, you’ll write frequently at a small scale, with guided “informal writings” leading to short papers that hone distinct skills, starting with close verbal analysis and then scaling up to think about form, genre, and context. As time permits, we’ll read samples of criticism to ask what makes a critical argument; use online reference tools to personalize your discoveries; and historical context to help texts speak anew to contemporary concerns. Authors to be read include Edgar Allen Poe, Virginia Woolf, Sandra Cisneros, Octavia Butler, Juliette Carrillo, Ocean Vuong, Ada Limón. Requirements: timely reading and lively participation; 3 informal writings (1 page) leading into 3 papers (2, 3, 6 pages); attendance and response to two specific live stage performances outside of class time; in-person open-book final exam.
